newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICA SAYS TAIWAN SUSPENSION 'MOST REGRETTABLE'.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICA SAYS TAIWAN SUSPENSION 'MOST REGRETTABLE'.

text.p: South Africa said on Thursday Taiwan's decision to withdraw its ambassador and immediately suspend all aid projects and treaties with Pretoria as a protest against a breakoff in diplomatic ties was "most regrettable".
Chang told state radio the decision was taken to register the island state's displeasure at Pretoria's decision to cancel full links with Taipei from 1997 in favour of Beijing.

Speaking after talks with South African Foreign Minister Alfred Nzo in Pretoria, Chang, who was reported to be visibly angry, said Taiwan would suspend its aid programme in South Africa and the bulk of the 36 existing treaties and agreements between the two countries.
He added he would meet Taiwanese businessmen on Friday to discuss the issue further.

"It is most regrettable that the government of the Republic of china (Taiwan) has reacted in the manner indicated by their foreign minister earlier today," South Africa's foreign affairs ministry said in a statement.
"...The reaction will influence our sincere desire that the friendly relations that have been built up over the years should continue to (our) mutual benefit.
"We reiterate that we would like to conduct our relations after 1997 at the highest level, short of diplomatic relations," the ministry said.

Acknowledging Taiwan's unhappiness over the decision, the ministry conceded: "It is, however, the prerogative of the government of the Republic of China to determine their response to this notification of the intended change of status in our relations."

Taiwan is South Africa's seventh-largest trading partner with two-way trade totalling 5.7 billion rand ($1.24 billion) in 1995. At least 43,000 jobs are expected to be lost if Taiwan disinvests entirely from South Africa.

One investment seen almost sure to be jeopardised by the diplomatic shift is a $3.5 billion petrochemicals plant, which was suggested by Taiwanese vice-premier Hsu Li-teh during an official visit to South Africa in August.

President Nelson Mandela told reporters after meeting Chang on Wednesday he would stick by his "agonising" decision to end diplomatic relations with Taiwan, but promised to maintain ties in all but name.
He said too that he was encouraged by remarks by business leaders in Taipei that the end of formal relations would not affect major Taiwanese investments in South Africa.
South Africa was Taiwan's biggest diplomatic ally, and its defection to Beijing leaves Taipei with diplomatic relations with just 29 nations, most of them small and poor, which receive Taiwanese aid.

Its relations with Taiwan date back to the apartheid era when both were diplomatic pariahs. The Taiwanese ambassador, Loh I-Cheng, is dean of the diplomatic corps in Pretoria, a 45-year veteran of the foreign service who knows Mandela personally.
Trade between South Africa and mainland China, which insists Taiwan is a renegade province, totalled $1.3 billion in 1995, up from just $14 million in 1991.
